topic.title: The 6 levels of money in India: which one are you?

title: The 6 levels of money in India: which one are you?
description:
Salary on the 1st, almost nothing left by the 25th. Which money level are you on, and what is the one move that gets you to the next?
Rohan climbs six money levels, from paycheck to paycheck to the floor where money earns more than he spends. Every floor has a trap that pushes people back down, priced in rupees with real maths.
Comment your level.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:27 Paycheck to paycheck
1:31 The cushion
2:43 Debt-free
4:17 Your money gets a job
5:21 The crore
6:24 Money does the work
7:24 Which one are you?

Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions.
Illustrative only. Not financial advice.

lines.text: Salary day was three weeks ago. Rohan has already spent ₹40,000, and his account is almost empty. At 6% inflation, in ten years the same month could cost ₹71,634.
Where does it all go? Every single month!
Here is the thing. There are six levels of money, and almost everyone starts on the first two.
By the end, you will know which level you are on, the trap waiting on every floor, and the one move that takes you up.
And the last level? It is not about earning more. You will see.
Think of it as a road with six signposts. Rohan is standing at the very first one.
On level one, ₹40,000 comes in, and ₹40,000 goes out. Every single month, back to zero.
Rent on the first. Food delivery all week. A friend's wedding on the twentieth. And by the twenty fifth, he is counting coins.
Even Sikka has nothing left to cheer about.
Rohan, what happens if your job stops next month?
Next month? I would be broke in a week.
And that is normal. Most first jobs start right here, so level one is not a failure. Staying here is the problem.
And a raise alone does not fix it. When the salary goes up, the spending quietly follows. A bigger flat, a nicer phone, more dinners out.
Because here is the trap of level one. Prices never stand still. At 6% inflation a year, the life that costs ₹40,000 a month today will cost ₹71,634.
Watch the cost of the same life climb, year after year. Nothing new in his cart. Just the same rent, the same food, the same bills.
That is ₹31,634 more every month. And over ten years, ₹19.1 L extra, just to live exactly the same life.
So your salary has to rise every year, just to stand still.
The move off level one is boring, and it works. Spend a little less than you earn, and keep the gap somewhere you will not touch.
Do that for long enough, and he reaches level two. The floor where most people think they are finally safe.
On level two, six months of spending, ₹2,40,000, sitting safely in a fixed deposit.
How big should a cushion be? The usual rule is three to six months of spending. Rohan goes for six, because his job is new.
Six months covered! I am basically rich now!
Not rich, Rohan. Safe. That is a different thing.
And safe matters. If the job stops, the cushion pays the rent while he finds the next one. No loan, no panic, no card.
So level two is a must. But it hides a quiet trap, and it is the reason so many people never climb past it.
The fixed deposit pays 7% a year. But prices are rising at 6%. So most of the interest just keeps up with prices.
Ten years go by. He never touches it. The FD keeps renewing, quietly.
On paper, it has grown to ₹4.7 L. Almost double. It looks wonderful.
But in today's money, after ten years of rising prices, it buys what ₹2.6 L buys now. The green line is the paper. The red line is what it can actually buy.
His real growth? About 0.9% a year. Ten years of saving, and his cushion barely grew at all.
And if he had kept it as cash at home? In today's money it would be worth just ₹1.3 L. Rising prices quietly take ₹1.1 L.
A cushion is for falling on. It was never meant for growing.
So the move on level two: keep the cushion, and stop adding to it once it is full. Every rupee after that needs a different job.
But first, there is one trap that knocks people from level two straight back down to level one. And it fits in your wallet.
Level three is simple. You owe nobody. Then a festive sale arrives, and Rohan puts ₹50,000 on his credit card.
The bill arrives. Total due, ₹50,000. Minimum due, just ₹2,500.
So he does what millions of people do. He pays the minimum.
Only ₹2,500? Easy. Bill paid!
But the card charges 3.5% a month on everything still owed.
That sounds small. Over a year, it is 42%. And because interest lands on interest, it really works out to about 51%.
Twelve months go by. Rohan pays every minimum, on time, not once late.
By now he has paid ₹27,385. And he still owes ₹40,826.
What? I paid more than half of it already!
Because ₹18,211 of what he paid went straight to interest. Only the rest touched the actual debt.
And the minimum shrinks as the balance shrinks, so the road goes on and on. Year after year, the debt walks beside him.
It takes 183 monthly payments. That is about 15 years.
All in, he pays ₹1.4 L to clear ₹50,000. That is about 2.9× what he spent.
In my bank days, we had a name for people who pay only the minimum. Our best customers.
And that is how one sale pushes a person back down. Every month, part of his salary belongs to the card, and he is back on level one.
Even converting the bill into a one year EMI at 16% would cost about ₹4,439 in interest. The minimum road costs ₹93,871.
The move on level three. Pay the total due every month, with autopay. Never take cash from a card.
If you truly cannot, a short EMI beats the minimum. And spend on the card only what is already in your account.
So that is three floors. Spend less than you earn. Build the cushion. Owe nobody.
And on the next floor, something changes. For the first time, your money starts climbing on its own.
On level four, Rohan invests ₹10,000 a month, every month, for 5 years. Not into the cushion this time, into investments.
The usual way in India is a SIP. A fixed amount goes into a mutual fund on the same date, every month, on autopilot.
But ₹10,000 every month? That is a lot.
Then start with less. The habit matters more than the amount. Raise it with every raise.
We will assume 12% a year. That is an assumption, not a promise. Markets swing.
Five years of the same date, the same amount. Good months, bad months, he keeps paying in.
He put in ₹6.0 L. It is now worth about ₹8.2 L.
That difference, ₹2.2 L, is money he never worked a single shift for.
It made ₹2.2 L without me doing anything?
Not without you. You kept paying in, even in the months it went down.
Here is the honest catch. Some years the value will fall, sometimes a lot. The people who climb further are the ones who do not stop.
Why does it grow? Returns earn returns. This year's growth joins the pile, and next year the pile grows on that too.
Like a pile of cash that keeps adding to itself. Small at first. And the longer you leave it, the bigger it gets.
So the move on level four: automate it. The SIP leaves on salary day, before you can spend it.
Now watch what happens when you give the very same habit a lot more time.
On level five, it is ₹15,000 a month, for 20 years. Same idea, just a longer hill.
Twenty years. Four phones, two jobs, one wedding. And the SIP never stops.
At year ten, the pot has reached ₹34.9 L. Nice, but not life changing. Then the second ten years begin.
At year twenty, it is ₹1.50 Cr. A crore and a half, from ₹15,000 a month.
A crorepati? Me?
Now the painful part. Start the same SIP ten years late, and you reach only ₹34.9 L. The same monthly amount.
Same Rohan. Same salary. Same SIP. The only difference is the year he started.
Most of that crore arrives in the last ten years. Waiting does not cost you the first ten years. It costs you the last ten.
Time does the heavy lifting. Not the amount.
And the honest catch. Remember the cushion? Prices keep rising, so a crore in twenty years buys a lot less than a crore today.
So the move on level five is the cheapest one in this whole video. Start now, even small, and do not stop.
And every year you wait, the finish line moves further away. To catch up later, the monthly amount has to be much bigger, right when life gets more expensive.
Five floors now. And the last one is not about having more money. It is about what your money does while you sleep.
Level six. Of that ₹1.50 Cr, only ₹36.0 L ever came from his salary. The other ₹1.14 Cr was the money working.
This is my floor. My money goes to work before I wake up.
Level six needs a much bigger pot than that. Say ₹8,00,00,000. At an assumed 8% a year, it grows by about ₹64.0 L in a single year.
Twenty years from now, at 6% inflation, Rohan's life costs about ₹15,39,425 a year. The growth is bigger than the bill.
So the money pays the bills, and the job becomes optional?
That is the idea. But nobody jumps here. Every floor below has to hold.
And one last honest catch. Returns are never guaranteed, and a bad year can wipe the growth out. So people here spend less than the full growth, and let the rest keep up with prices.
Which is exactly why people on level six still keep the cushion, and still owe nobody. The lower floors never go away.
And Sharma Uncle did not get here in one jump. He climbed every floor, one boring month at a time, for decades.
So level six is three things at once. A cushion. No debt. And a pot so big that its growth covers the bills, with room to spare.
So, which floor are you on? And one move on that floor matters more than all the others.
Now be honest with yourself. Not the level you wish you were on. The one your bank account says you are on today.
Walk the road with Rohan. Each signpost is a floor. Stop at the one that sounds like your life today.
Level one, the month ends before the money. Your move: spend less than you earn.
Level two, you have a cushion. Your move: keep it, and stop there.
Level three, nobody owns your salary. Your move: pay the total due, every single month.
Level four, you invest. Your move: automate it.
Level five, time is on your side. Your move: do not stop.
And level six, keep every floor below you standing.
And the move that matters most is the cheapest one: start early. Same ₹15,000 a month. Start now, ₹1.50 Cr. Start ten years late, ₹34.9 L.
I am on level two. Next stop, a card I pay in full, and a SIP on salary day.
And wherever you are, the next floor is one move away. Not six. Just one.
Just one? Fine. Starting this month.
Our maths is simplified, before tax and fees, so real life will be messier. So, which level are you on? Comment your number. And follow the panchayat for one money question, settled with real maths.

Beat l6-more (with l6-year, l6-rohan, l6-sharma2): 'That is more than Rohan spends in a whole year, even at ₹40,000 a month. The money now earns more than the life costs' compares year-20 nominal growth (₹12.0 L at 8% on ₹1.50 Cr) with TODAY's spending. By the video's own 6% inflation (l1-trap, l5-honest) the same life costs about ₹1.28 L a month, ~₹15.4 L a year, by year 20, so the growth does NOT cover it; and spending all 8% growth while prices rise 6% shrinks the pot in real terms (real growth ~2%, before tax). The conclusion the numbers do not support (rule 3), and Rohan 'the job becomes optional' / Sharma 'That is the idea' builds on it. Fix: compare like with like: add a price_rise maths for ₹40,000 at 6% over 20 years and show the year-20 cost next to the growth, or move the comparison to today's money (real_return), or make the level-6 pot large enough that its growth covers the year-20 cost and say a sustainable draw is well below the full nominal return; reword l6-more so it is true under the stated assumptions.

Note (not a reject): open beat says the same month 'will cost ₹71,634' as a certainty; better 'at 6% inflation, could cost' (l1-trap already words it as an assumption). l3-down 'The cushion goes into the card' sits oddly with 15 years of minimums; l3/l3-fork omit 18% GST on card interest and EMI-conversion processing fees (both make the minimum road worse, so not misleading). FD at 7%: SBI general-public top rate is 6.80% (5-10y 6.05%), within the channel's 6-7.5% band; 6% inflation fits Sept 2026 CPI 5.54% (MoSPI). 3.5%/month and 5% minimum due match issuer MITCs (Bajaj/IndusInd 3.5%, IndusInd MAD 5%). Description 'Chapters' list is empty until render fills timestamps; disclaimer present at the end.

Beats l6-year/l6-more/l6-catch with l6-rohan/l6-sharma2 (re-review): the like-for-like comparison is now right (₹24.0 L growth on ₹3 Cr at 8% vs ₹15,39,425 a year of life in year 20 at 6%), but l6-catch's remedy contradicts the video's own numbers. Spending ₹15.4 L of the ₹24.0 L leaves ₹8.6 L, while keeping ₹3 Cr level with 6% inflation needs ₹18 L a year. So 'spend less than the full growth, and let the rest keep up with prices' is impossible at this pot, the pot shrinks in real terms every year, and 'the job becomes optional?' / 'That is the idea' is still not supported (rule 3). The real return is about 2% (8% vs 6%), so a pot whose growth covers the bill AND keeps up with prices needs about ₹15.4 L / 0.02 = ~₹7.7 Cr (before tax). Fix: either raise the rich pot to about ₹8 Cr (say ₹8,00,00,000: ₹64 L growth, ₹48 L to keep up with prices, ₹16 L left > ₹15.4 L bill) and keep the lines, or keep ₹3 Cr and reword l6-more/l6-catch/l6-sharma2 honestly (the growth covers the bill for now, but to also keep up with prices the pot must be far bigger, so level six is a direction, not a finish line), with no 'job becomes optional' / 'That is the idea' endorsement at ₹3 Cr.
